extracted.intended_audience: business managers, CSR practitioners, policymakers, students and researchers interested in corporate social responsibility
extracted.subtask_description: A broad set of practices, metrics, legal rules, and evaluative dimensions for designing, implementing, measuring, and judging corporate social responsibility (CSR) and a company's Social License to Operate across jurisdictions and supply chains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the business strategy and business objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: To achieve the goal (of a Social License to Operate / CSR aims), a company needs to identify the business strategy and business objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational step before mapping stakeholders or CSR activities; objectives should be explicit so that desired support from stakeholders can be specified and measured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify social license holders (stakeholder mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the social license holders (employees of a company, labour unions, local and national governments, communities, activist groups, etc.) for every business objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholder identification must be done per business objective (not just globally) and include all groups that can grant or withhold social acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specify social license elements for each objective
rubrics_metrics.description: For every business objective, specify the social license element (target of support, context of support, time of support, action of support).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be precise about what support is desired (who, when, in what context, and what actions are expected) to make measurement and strategy design possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitatively measure stakeholder intention to support
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantitatively measure the intention (positive or negative) of the social license holders to support the business objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surveys, metrics or other instruments to capture stakeholders' intention and track changes over time rather than relying solely on qualitative impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify negative factors affecting stakeholder intention
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the factors that negatively impact the intention of the social license holders to support the business objectives (strength of their belief in support, their evaluation of support outcomes, the pressure to provide support, enablers/disablers of support, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnose barriers, misperceptions, competing pressures and operational enablers/disablers so interventions can be targeted; consider psychological and contextual drivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a Social License Development Strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop the Social License Development Strategy to remove the negative factors and ensure the positive intention of all the social license holders to support all the company's business objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy should be tailored to identified stakeholders and their negative factors, and should align with business objectives and measurable social license elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ongoing monitoring and quantitative measurement of Social License to Operate
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform ongoing monitoring and quantitative measurement of changes in the Social License to Operate of the company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous measurement enables detection of shifts in stakeholder intention and the effectiveness of interventions; this is an iterative process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for emerging vs developed market contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine CSR results under different lenses for emerging and developed economies, since governance, stakeholder expectations and impacts differ by context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In emerging markets, CSR can enable broader market reach and reputational benefits but firms may face weak firm-level governance; tailor CSR approaches to local institutional conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triple bottom line (People, Planet, Profit)
rubrics_metrics.description: "People, planet, and profit" form one way to evaluate CSR: 'People' covers fair labour and community, 'Planet' sustainable environmental practices, and 'Profit' the economic value created net of input costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balancing economic, ecological, and social goals is central; be aware of criticisms (selectivity, lack of standard auditing) and document assumptions and measurement methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human resources and employee engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use CSR programs to aid recruitment and retention, improve staff perception, enable payroll giving, fundraising, community volunteering, and encourage customer orientation among employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure employee engagement in CSR initiatives; engage employees meaningfully (not tokenistically) to influence turnover, morale, productivity and employer brand.

rubrics_metrics.name: CSR as risk management and reputational protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement CSR to limit risks to reputation, reduce regulatory/legal exposure, and increase resilience across value chains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High CSR compliance across supply chains (including beyond Tier 1) reduces vulnerabilities; CSR can preempt lawsuits and regulatory interventions and should be integrated into risk-management processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supply chain and procurement sustainability
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage sustainability-focused procurement and supplier relations: look for suppliers that share social, environmental and ethics values to reduce risks and create shared innovations and value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that up to 70% of social and environmental impacts may occur in the supply chain; procurement strategy should balance price with CSR expectations and extend monitoring beyond Tier 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand differentiation and consumer perception factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use CSR to enhance brand reputation but account for factors that moderate effects (consumers' valuation of relationships, perceived self-serving motives, perceived product-quality impacts, consumption-related goals, and attributions about motives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communications should avoid appearing self-serving; consider how CSR positioning may affect product evaluations and purchasing behavior under different consumer motivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages/maturity model of CSR practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Three stages: (1) philanthropy (donations, volunteering), (2) improving operational effectiveness (sustainability to reduce costs, employee conditions), (3) transforming the business model (creating new businesses addressing social/environmental challenges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess where the company sits on this continuum; examples: Coca‑Cola and PNC for philanthropy, Grupo Bimbo for operational effectiveness, Unilever Project Shakti and IKEA People & Planet for business-model transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced regulatory scrutiny as a potential CSR outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: A CSR program can persuade governments and the public that a company takes health & safety, diversity, and the environment seriously, potentially reducing close monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a possible benefit but not guaranteed — ensure transparency and substance to avoid accusations of misdirection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis management via stakeholder engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use CSR-related relationship-building and meeting local stakeholders' social expectations to mitigate crises (e.g., responses to boycotts, post-conflict support, philanthropic assistance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples (Arla Foods, Citibank) show that targeted support for local priorities helps regain trust; ongoing local engagement is crucial for resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess and disclose motives and avoid hypocrisy
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether CSR activities are driven by genuine social/environmental aims or by self-serving motives (reputational management, distraction from core harms), since perceived motives influence stakeholder response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency in motives, measurement of outcomes, and alignment with core business practices reduce accusations of hypocrisy or greenwashing; consumers respond less favorably to initiatives believed to be self-serving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider leadership ethical ideologies and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that CEOs' political/ethical ideologies and company financial performance influence CSR preferences and emphasis (liberal vs conservative tendencies toward CSR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess leadership values and incentive structures as part of CSR strategy design — these influence which CSR activities are prioritized and their sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against misdirection and greenwashing
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that companies may use CSR or corporate social marketing to direct attention away from harmful practices; such misdirection increases consumer cynicism and mistrust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid superficial campaigns that do not address core harms; ensure rigorous evidence and independent verification to maintain credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special scrutiny for controversial industries
rubrics_metrics.description: Industries producing harmful products (tobacco, alcohol, munitions) complicate CSR assessments because philanthropic activity coexists with core product harms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate CSR in light of core business impacts; philanthropy may not offset product harms and can be seen as legitimacy-seeking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal and reporting compliance (jurisdictional rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comply with jurisdictional CSR-related laws and reporting requirements (e.g., Denmark's requirement for large companies to include CSR/SRI policies, implementation, results and management expectations in financial reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map local legal requirements and ensure disclosures cover policies, implementation practices and measurable results; lack of policy may require a statement of position in some jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory CSR spending and governance (India example)
rubrics_metrics.description: In India (Companies Act 2013), qualifying companies must spend at least 2% of average net profits on CSR and establish a CSR committee to oversee spending; thresholds are defined by net worth, turnover or profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal compliance requires governance structures and documented spending; note India’s approach treats CSR more as philanthropic community development within its legal framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: EU/RBC integration and strategic actions
rubrics_metrics.description: The EU model recommends that enterprises integrate social, environmental, ethical, human rights and consumer concerns into business operations and core strategy and pursue actions like enhancing CSR visibility, improving trust tracking, improving disclosure, and aligning national/global approaches (2011–14 agenda).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt processes for integration with stakeholder collaboration, improve disclosure practices, participate in self- and co-regulation, and align company strategy with regional/national CSR agendas.

rubrics_metrics.name: CSR performance assessment axes (human, product, environmental responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess CSR performance across areas such as human responsibility (supplier working conditions, employee treatment), product responsibility (content disclosure, country of origin, liability), and environmental responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three axes (or similar) as evaluative categories when measuring and reporting CSR performance; provide specific indicators for each axis (e.g., labour standards, product labeling, emissions).
